wiki_links.section: Phase VIII: PKB Connections & Cross-Report Links
wiki_links.context_line: > - **[[Schema-Automation]]** — Schema automation in the reading context provides the mechanism by which practice transforms effortful decoding into automatic recognition. This analysis shows schema automation operating on orthographic patterns — a concrete domain for a concept that is sometimes discussed abstractly. The connection is also predictive: whatever interferes with schema automation (insufficient practice volume, over-reliance on context guessing that bypasses orthographic processing) should impair fluency development.

wiki_links.section: Phase VIII: PKB Connections & Cross-Report Links
wiki_links.context_line: > - **[[Dual-Process-Theory]]** — The automaticity-liberation framework maps cleanly onto Type 1/Type 2 processing: fluent word recognition is a Type 1 process operating outside conscious attention; comprehension strategy deployment is a Type 2 process requiring deliberate attentional resources. Fluency is the mechanism by which reading's most critical lower-level process transitions from Type 2 to Type 1, enabling higher-order Type 2 processing to operate unimpeded.

wiki_links.section: Phase VIII: PKB Connections & Cross-Report Links
wiki_links.context_line: > - **[[Matthew-Effect]]** — This analysis provides the cognitive-mechanistic account of why early reading skill gaps compound: the bottleneck mechanism guarantees that lower-skill readers extract less learning from equivalent reading time, creating a cognitive (not merely motivational) basis for the Matthew Effect's operation. The Matthew Effect note likely focuses on the behavioral and motivational dynamics; this analysis adds the architectural explanation.

wiki_links.section: Phase VIII: PKB Connections & Cross-Report Links
wiki_links.context_line: > - **[[Focal-Subsidiary-Attention-Distinction]]** — The transition from reading words focally to reading through words subsidiarily is the phenomenological description of the automaticity development process this report analyzes mechanistically. The Polanyi framework provides the phenomenological language for what CLT and automaticity theory describe architecturally.

wiki_links.section: Phase VIII: PKB Connections & Cross-Report Links
wiki_links.context_line: > - **[[Procedural-Memory]]** — Automatized reading skills are procedural in character: fast, non-conscious, resistant to degradation under dual-task conditions. The procedural memory note connects to the mechanism through which practiced decoding becomes automatic — the long-term memory encoding of orthographic processing routines that operate without working memory recruitment.

wiki_links.section: Phase VIII: PKB Connections & Cross-Report Links
wiki_links.context_line: > - **[[Fluency-Illusion]]** — The fluency-metacognition paradox identified in Phase VI connects directly to the Fluency Illusion: disfluent readers cannot reliably distinguish between genuine comprehension and the illusion of comprehension, because both the comprehension process and its monitoring draw on the same depleted working memory pool.

wiki_links.section: Phase VIII: PKB Connections & Cross-Report Links
wiki_links.context_line: > - **[[Dreyfus-Skill-Acquisition-Model]]** — The novice-to-expert transition in reading follows the Dreyfus model precisely: novices focus explicitly on decoding rules; experts process meaning holistically. This analysis grounds the Dreyfus model's phenomenological description in specific cognitive mechanisms (working memory, schema automation) that explain *why* the transition from rule-following to intuitive performance occurs.

wiki_links.context_line: > **Synthetic Observation**: The pattern of connections reveals that reading fluency and automaticity is a domain-specific worked example of a set of domain-general architectural principles — [[Working-Memory]] constraints, [[Schema-Automation]], [[Dual-Process-Theory]], and the [[Focal-Subsidiary-Attention-Distinction]] — that operate across all hierarchically organized skills. wiki_links.section: A. Lexicon of Key Terms
wiki_links.context_line: > The [[Phonological-Loop]] is the component of working memory that maintains verbal information in a phonological (sound-based) code through active rehearsal. It holds approximately 3-4 items for approximately 2 seconds without rehearsal. In reading, the phonological loop maintains the sound representations of recently decoded words while subsequent words are processed — making it the critical resource for sentence-level integration. Non-automatic decoding consumes phonological loop resources, leaving insufficient capacity for maintaining sentence-length phonological representations.
